pglmm_matrix_structure produces the entire covariance matrix structure (V) when you specify random effects.

Source: R/pglmm-utils.R
pglmm-matrix-structure.Rd

pglmm_matrix_structure produces the entire covariance matrix structure (V) when you specify random effects.

Usage

pglmm_matrix_structure(
  formula,
  data = list(),
  family = "binomial",
  cov_ranef,
  repulsion = FALSE,
  ss = 1,
  cpp = TRUE
)

communityPGLMM.matrix.structure(
  formula,
  data = list(),
  family = "binomial",
  cov_ranef,
  repulsion = FALSE,
  ss = 1,
  cpp = TRUE
)

Arguments

formula

A two-sided linear formula object describing the mixed effects of the model.

To specify that a random term should have phylogenetic covariance matrix along with non-phylogenetic one, add __ (two underscores) at the end of the group variable; e.g., + (1 | sp__) will construct two random terms, one with phylogenetic covariance matrix and another with non-phylogenetic (identity) matrix. In contrast, __ in the nested terms (below) will only create a phylogenetic covariance matrix. Nested random terms have the general form (1|sp__@site__) which represents phylogenetically related species nested within correlated sites. This form can be used for bipartite questions. For example, species could be phylogenetically related pollinators and sites could be phylogenetically related plants, leading to the random effect (1|insects__@plants__). If more than one phylogeny is used, remember to add all to the argument cov_ranef = list(insects = insect_phylo, plants = plant_phylo). Phylogenetic correlations can be dropped by removing the __ underscores. Thus, the form (1|sp@site__) excludes the phylogenetic correlations among species, while the form (1|sp__@site) excludes the correlations among sites.

Note that correlated random terms are not allowed. For example, (x|g) will be the same as (0 + x|g) in the lme4::lmer syntax. However, (x1 + x2|g) won't work, so instead use (x1|g) + (x2|g), or (x1 + x2||g). As the random intercept and slope of (1|g) + (x|g) are independent, the model depends on where x is zero: the variance among the levels of g is that of the intercept plus \(x^2\) times that of the slope. With a 0/1 covariate (e.g. a control and a treatment), the levels then vary more in the treatment than in the control by construction. Center continuous covariates of random slopes (e.g. x - mean(x)) and code two-level factors as -1/+1 (equal variance in both groups) unless zero is a meaningful reference. Covariates of random slopes must be numeric columns of data.

Grouping factors are columns of data. Their interactions as in lme4, e.g. (1|sp:site), are fitted as the nested terms (1|sp@site), and (1|site/sp) as (1|site) + (1|sp@site).

The formula can have offsets, e.g. + offset(log(effort)) for counts with different sampling efforts or areas: terms of the linear predictor with a known coefficient of one. They are supported with method = "Laplace" (binomial, poisson and negative binomial models) and bayes = TRUE, and are included in the predicted values (predict(), fitted(), simulate(); with newdata, the offset is calculated from it).

data

A data.frame containing the variables named in formula. Rows with missing values in the response, the fixed effects, the grouping variables or the covariates of random slopes are dropped before fitting; this is equivalent to removing those rows from data manually before calling pglmm. As a result, pglmm(data_with_NAs) and pglmm(na.omit(data[, vars])) (with vars the variables of the model) produce identical estimates. With random.effects, only the rows with missing values in the response are dropped.

family

Either "gaussian" for a Linear Mixed Model, or "binomial", "poisson", "nbinomial" or "Gamma" for Generalized Linear Mixed Models. "family" should be specified as a character string (i.e., quoted). For binomial and Poisson data, we use the canonical logit and log link functions, respectively. Binomial data can be either presence/absence, or a two-column array of 'successes' and 'failures'. For both binomial and Poisson data, we add an observation-level random term by default via add.obs.re = TRUE.

"nbinomial" is the negative binomial distribution for overdispersed counts, with the log link and the variance \(\mu + \mu^2 / \theta\) given the random effects (as lme4::glmer.nb(), glmmTMB(family = nbinom2) and MASS::glm.nb()). Its dispersion parameter \(\theta\) is estimated with the other parameters (element theta of the fitted model); \(\theta = \infty\) is the poisson distribution. As \(\theta\) accounts for overdispersion, no observation-level random term is added. With bayes = FALSE, negative binomial models are always fitted with method = "Laplace", with starting values from MASS::glm.nb().

"Gamma" (or "gamma") is the Gamma distribution for positive continuous responses (e.g. biomass, body size, durations), with the log link and the variance \(\mu^2 / \nu\) given the random effects (as glm(), lme4::glmer() and glmmTMB() with family = Gamma(link = "log")). Its shape parameter \(\nu\) is estimated with the other parameters (element shape of the fitted model; sigma() of glmmTMB is \(1/\sqrt{\nu}\), the coefficient of variation). No observation-level random term is added. Gamma models are only available with bayes = FALSE, and are always fitted with method = "Laplace", with starting values from glm() and MASS::gamma.shape().

If bayes = TRUE there are three additional families available: "zeroinflated.binomial", "zeroinflated.poisson" and "zeroinflated.nbinomial", which add a zero inflation parameter; this parameter gives the probability that the response is a zero. The rest of the parameters of the model then reflect the "non-zero" part part of the model. Note that "zeroinflated.binomial" only makes sense for success/failure response data.

cov_ranef

A named list of covariance matrices of random terms. The names should be the group variables that are used as random terms with specified covariance matrices (without the two underscores, e.g. list(sp = tree1, site = tree2)). The actual object can be either a phylogeny with class "phylo" or a prepared covariance matrix. If it is a phylogeny, pglmm will prune it and then convert it to a covariance matrix assuming Brownian motion evolution. pglmm will also standardize all covariance matrices to have determinant of one (unless standardize_cov = FALSE), so the estimated variances of these terms are on the scale of the standardized matrices; use scale_factors of the fitted model to rescale them (see "Extracting the variances of random terms" in Details). Group variables will be converted to factors and all covariance matrices will be rearranged so that rows and columns are in the same order as the levels of their corresponding group variables.

repulsion

When there are nested random terms specified, repulsion = FALSE tests for phylogenetic underdispersion while repulsion = TRUE tests for overdispersion. This argument is a logical vector of length either 1 or >1. If its length is 1, it applies to the phylogenies of species only (the variable before @, e.g. sp in sp__@site and sp__@site__): their covariance matrices are either inverted (overdispersion) or not, while the phylogenies of sites (after @) are never inverted. This follows Ives and Helmus (2011, Appendix A), where repulsion arises from competition among closely related species. If it has more than one element, then you can select which covariance matrix in the nested terms to be inverted. Make sure to get the length right: for all the terms with @, count the number of "__" to determine the length of repulsion. For example, sp__@site and sp@site__ will each require one element of repulsion, while sp__@site__ will take two elements (repulsion for sp and repulsion for site). Therefore, if your nested terms are (1|sp__@site) + (1|sp@site__) + (1|sp__@site__), then you should set the repulsion to be something like c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE) (length of 4).

ss

Which of the random.effects to produce.

cpp

Whether to use C++ function for optim. Default is TRUE. Only used by the dense code (sparse = FALSE, which is the default only for models that the sparse code does not support, see sparse); ignored if bayes = TRUE, sparse = TRUE or method = "Laplace" (and thus for family = "nbinomial" and "Gamma"): these models are fitted with R code, with the sparse Cholesky factorizations of the Matrix package (CHOLMOD).

Value

A design matrix.
